subtitle: Disagreements with community partners carry personally learned meanings. Understand them, clarify what real participation looks like and follow through with an honest account of how input was used.
scope: For staff across DHS. Original practice adult examples distinguish an engagement proposal, chosen personal meanings, actual responsibilities and supported feedback. This course does not grant representative, service, procurement or decision authority, promise a community’s agreement, administer an IDI assessment or diagnose a person’s culture. Native American and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the person or area responsible within ADSA.
introTranscript: A disagreement with a community partner may concern both the practical plan and the meaning of a respectful exchange. Follow Tobin and Edda as they consider a practice public-information discussion. Examine their particular expectations, change a first interpretation, clarify how contributions could influence the work and distinguish feedback from a claim of community agreement. Private self-understanding can matter alongside appropriate work application.

intro.heading: Identify the disagreement without judging the partner
intro.body:
Tobin is a practice DHS staff member considering a public-information discussion with Edda, a practice adult community partner. No event, service change, funding or binding engagement process has been approved in this case. Tobin proposes questions early in the discussion; Edda proposes letting a contributor finish an opening account before questions. They agree that people should be able to contribute, but disagree about how that contribution should begin.

Tobin first reads Edda’s proposal as turning participants into a passive audience. Edda first reads Tobin’s proposal as breaking up an account before its meaning can be understood. These are initial interpretations, not established motives. The case has not shown that Edda refuses questions, that Tobin dismisses community knowledge or that everyone who might attend shares either view. The disagreement needs explanation at the level of the actual proposal.

Minnesota’s Office of Collaboration and Dispute Resolution describes meaningful public engagement as relationship and dialogue, including deeper concerns and participation rather than a single communication. It also recognizes that agreement on every aspect may not be possible. This public guidance helps frame the inquiry; it does not appoint either person to a formal facilitation role or establish an internal DHS approval chain.

Edda’s partner role is particular. Her contribution may be valuable without being the view of an entire community or a delegation to decide an agency issue. Likewise, Tobin’s staff role does not by itself establish power to commit resources or promise a final change. Ask what the discussion is for, whose perspectives are being sought and what influence is actually available. Those questions make the disagreement more understandable without prejudging its answer.

Privately separate the proposed methods from the first judgments. You may reflect on what makes a partnership feel respectful to you, without sharing a personal history or entering a real conflict. The full example is an equally valid path. A better understanding of your own assumptions is worthwhile even if no event is organized.

flashcards.back: A person or organization contributing in a particular role; the role does not automatically represent every affected person.
Different views about how an exchange should work, distinct from a finding that someone is unwilling or incapable.
A chosen account of what a practice means to this person, rather than a cultural group rule.

items.title: Name the actual difference
items.body: Early questions and a completed opening account are different proposals for beginning the exchange. Saying Edda opposes participation goes further than the supplied difference. Ask how questions would be included rather than treating a proposed sequence as proof that she wants an audience without a voice.

items.title: Keep the partner role particular
items.body: Edda may contribute a perspective and help develop a plan. That does not establish authority to represent every person affected or decide for the agency. A respectful partnership asks which role is intended and whose views remain missing rather than treating one relationship as a complete community agreement.

items.title: Allow disagreement within engagement
items.body: A disagreement about method does not automatically make a partnership unsuccessful. It can identify different concerns worth examining. The public guidance supports fair dialogue without promising consensus; actual purpose, access, resources and decision responsibilities still need their real basis.

tabs.label: Explain the difference as a defect
tabs.body: Tobin calls Edda unwilling to engage because she proposes a completed account first. That judgment skips the reason behind the method. It may close a useful exchange before the purpose and question opportunities are understood, and the example supplies no such motive finding.

tabs.label: Treat one partner as the whole community
tabs.body: Accept Edda’s method as the community’s unanimous preference because she is a partner. This overstates both representation and agreement. Her actual contribution can be heard while other perspectives, particular participation needs and decision responsibilities remain to be examined.

tabs.label: Describe and inquire
tabs.body: Name the different proposals and ask what each is meant to preserve. This keeps the disagreement concrete and gives both people room to explain. It does not guarantee agreement or remove the need to clarify who participates, what influence is available and who decides.

check.question: Which statement matches the supplied disagreement?
check.correct: They differ about when questions begin; neither proposal establishes opposition to participation or universal representation.
wrong: Edda’s opening-account proposal proves she refuses questions.
Tobin’s staff role automatically authorizes any service change.
A community partnership means everyone affected agrees.
check.feedbackCorrect: The statement describes the actual method difference without inventing motives, authority or a community-wide result.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An opening account is not proof that questions are refused. A staff role does not establish every service decision power. Partnership does not supply everyone’s agreement; actual contributions and missing perspectives remain distinct.

lessons.statement: Hear the personally offered reason before equating a different sequence with exclusion.

intro.heading: Hear the meaning of a complete account
intro.body:
Edda voluntarily explains that, in an oral-history circle she joined, letting someone finish an opening account was a way of recognizing the person’s experience as a whole. Questions came afterward, when the listener could relate a detail to the complete account. For Edda, a finished opening can mean that the person is not merely being mined for fragments. It does not mean that no one may ask questions.

This supplied reason widens Tobin’s first interpretation. What looked like a passive-audience method can also express concern about faithful understanding and recognition. Tobin can now ask what completion would mean in this particular proposed discussion and how a contributor would choose to finish or invite questions. He should not translate the account into a rule that every oral-history participant dislikes interruption or that Edda represents all contributors.

The Council of Europe describes cultural meanings as personally interpreted and internally varied, and connects wider perspectives with a changed response. The new account therefore matters as Edda’s chosen reason in this exchange. It supplies neither an IDI placement nor a prediction about language, identity or ability. No contributor is required to disclose an intimate life history to establish the value of a practical concern.

A revised proposal could offer an opening contribution followed by questions at a point the contributor understands, with a clear opportunity to ask or decline further questions. This response takes the complete account seriously instead of continuing to call the method passive. It still needs examination against the purpose and actual participation needs. The case has not confirmed any contributor’s choice, the meeting period or the required supports.

Privately describe the first interpretation, Edda’s offered meaning and the change in response. You may recognize a personally meaningful experience of being heard, or simply use the example. Do not enter a sensitive account or ask someone else to explain their family or community. Understanding why recognition matters to you can be useful without organizing a discussion or proving a work result.

items.title: Recognize the whole account
items.body: Edda’s concern is that a contributor’s meaning be heard in context rather than reduced to disconnected fragments. That provides a reason to examine the opening method. It does not establish that an unlimited monologue is necessary or that every question is disrespectful; ask what the particular contributor would choose.

items.title: Widen without surrendering inquiry
items.body: Tobin can acknowledge recognition and still ask how other participants will ask questions. Understanding Edda’s reason changes the first judgment, not every practical responsibility. A fitting proposal preserves the account and makes the subsequent exchange understandable rather than treating respect as silence.

items.title: Keep recognition voluntary
items.body: A contributor may prefer a shorter opening or may not want a personal story at all. Giving the proposed account room should not become a demand for biography. The invitation can make options clear while preserving choice, actual purpose and appropriate information practices.

tabs.label: Keep the passive-audience label
tabs.body: Tobin hears Edda’s chosen reason but continues saying she does not want participation. This ignores the supplied explanation that questions follow the account. New information should widen the interpretation rather than become a decorative acknowledgment attached to the same negative judgment.

tabs.label: Make the method compulsory
tabs.body: Turn Edda’s account into a rule that every contributor must tell a full personal story before questions. This replaces a concern about recognition with forced disclosure and a universal method. Ask what a person actually wants to contribute instead of prescribing biography as authentic participation.

tabs.label: Preserve context and examine choice
tabs.body: Propose an understood opening contribution and a clear point for questions, with the person able to choose what to share. This responds to the supplied meaning while leaving actual timing, supports and participant response open. It does not claim the revised method has already been accepted.

check.question: What does Edda’s account support?
check.correct: Her proposed sequence can express recognition of a whole account, so Tobin should reconsider the passive-audience judgment.
wrong: Every community member must prefer questions only at the end.
Every contributor must disclose a personal life history.
Understanding Edda removes all practical participation questions.
check.feedbackCorrect: The chosen meaning provides a wider reading of this proposal without creating a group rule or ending practical inquiry.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Edda’s personal account is not everyone’s preference. Recognition does not require compulsory biography. Understanding the meaning leaves actual timing, choice, supports and participation questions to examine.

items.text: A completed account represented recognition to Edda.
Questions followed the account in her chosen experience.
Reconsider the passive-audience interpretation.
Clarify the point for questions and contribution choice.
Every participant must tell a personal history.
All community members prefer this sequence.

intro.heading: Hear why an early question can mean contribution
intro.body:
Tobin voluntarily explains his experience in a museum dialogue group. A question early in an exchange signaled that visitors were helping shape what would be examined, rather than receiving a finished account and commenting only afterward. For him, an early question can mean shared authorship of the inquiry. It does not mean that a contributor’s full account has no value or that he expects a person to reveal private experiences on demand.

Edda initially hears the early question as extracting fragments from an account. Tobin’s chosen explanation widens that reading: he is trying to make room for people to influence the direction. She can now distinguish a question that takes a story apart from a question about what participants want the exchange to examine. The actual wording and purpose matter; the word question alone does not settle the issue.

Neither meaning is a cultural ranking. Edda’s recognition concern and Tobin’s authorship concern can each be considered without assigning one person a fixed orientation or calling one method more advanced. The Council of Europe’s account of wider perspectives supports reconsidering one’s initial frame. Understanding another reason does not require abandoning one’s own affiliation or pretending the two experiences were the same.

A revised opening could ask participants what general questions they hope to explore, then offer a chosen account with an understood point for follow-up questions. This separates shaping the inquiry from interrupting a particular story. It is a new proposal, not a confirmed universal solution. Actual contributors can choose another method, and available time, language, access and information responsibilities still need examination.

Privately recognize how a question may have meant care, challenge or shared contribution in your own experience, without recording it. Or compare only Tobin and Edda’s complete fiction. The insight can enrich your understanding before a practical plan is accepted. No one owes a biography, a preferred public method or a workplace result to make that reflection worthwhile.

items.title: Distinguish kinds of questions
items.body: A question about what people want the discussion to examine differs from interrupting a contributor’s account to request a detail. The first can invite authorship of the inquiry; the second may need a different moment. Examine the actual purpose and wording instead of treating all early questions as equally respectful or disrespectful.

items.title: Make the widening reciprocal
items.body: Edda can recognize Tobin’s authorship concern while Tobin retains her recognition concern. This is not one person adapting and the other remaining the default. Both can reconsider the first judgment and propose a method that makes the particular contribution choices understandable.

items.title: Keep participation choices genuine
items.body: A revised opening should not require everyone to offer a question or story publicly. Someone may want to listen, use another available channel or decline a personal account. The case does not establish which supports are ready, so a proposal should identify those practical questions without predicting a person’s ability or preference.

tabs.label: Treat every question as extraction
tabs.body: Edda assumes that even a general invitation to shape the inquiry must fragment someone’s story. Tobin’s supplied reason gives a wider possibility. Ask what the actual question does rather than defending an initial interpretation as the only culturally respectful reading.

tabs.label: Treat authorship as compulsory speaking
tabs.body: Tobin requires every person to ask a question at the opening to prove engagement. This converts an opportunity into a performance gate. A useful invitation can make influence understandable while preserving people’s choice about contribution and actual participation needs.

tabs.label: Separate shaping the inquiry from interrupting an account
tabs.body: Offer a general opening question about what should be examined and a chosen account with an understood follow-up point. This responds to both meanings in a concrete way. It remains a proposal to consider, with actual support and contributor response open rather than universally guaranteed.

check.question: Which distinction fits Tobin’s offered meaning?
check.correct: A general question about what to examine can invite shared authorship without requiring interruption of a person’s account.
wrong: Every early question must disrespect a complete account.
Every participant must speak publicly to prove engagement.
Understanding Tobin requires Edda to abandon her recognition concern.
check.feedbackCorrect: The distinction uses the purpose of the actual question and preserves the other concern rather than prescribing a universal style.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Not every early question interrupts an account. Shared authorship is not compulsory public speaking. Edda can understand Tobin’s purpose while retaining a legitimate concern about recognition and choice.

lessons.statement: Make the available influence and actual decision responsibility understandable before asking for input.

image.caption: Two people review a printed document together; one points to a line on the page.

intro.heading: Clarify how input can affect the work
intro.body:
Tobin and Edda’s revised proposal is more understandable, but it still needs a clear purpose. Are they asking people what questions the public-information discussion should address, asking for feedback about a proposed explanation or inviting participation in a decision? Those are different tasks. The example has not supplied a service decision or delegated authority. A title such as partner or collaborative discussion does not create either.

MMB Management Analysis and Development advises explaining how input will be used and creating a feedback loop. This is practical public guidance, not a newly imposed universal DHS meeting method. Its useful question is whether a contributor can understand the actual purpose and what happens to the contribution. Tobin can describe a proposal honestly without saying that every suggestion will become the final arrangement.

The distinction matters in the example. If participants suggest questions for the discussion, organizers can consider those topics and later explain the choices. That is not the same as giving participants power to approve a service policy or assigning Edda ownership of staff work. A contribution may influence the plan; the record needs to show what actually changed rather than equate attendance or receipt with influence.

Practical participation also needs examination. The case has not established whose perspectives remain missing, the actual language and access needs or which contribution channels are available. Do not infer those facts from a person’s identity, affiliation, writing style or silence. A proposed method can be clearer while still needing actual support and appropriate handling of names or personal information. No universal anonymity or confidentiality promise is established.

Privately explain the difference among a contribution received, a contribution considered and an actual decision. You can use only the example. If you choose a work application, clarify the actual purpose, information responsibilities and decision-maker through the relevant process. The course does not authorize a change or require you to collect personal histories to prove that engagement was meaningful.

lessons.keyStatement: Make the available influence and actual decision responsibility understandable before asking for input.

items.title: Name the actual purpose of input
items.body: Suggesting topics for a public explanation differs from approving a policy. A contributor should not have to guess which task is available. Explain that distinction before asking for input; otherwise the same invitation may appear to promise a power the organizers have not established.

items.title: Show consideration without claiming automatic adoption
items.body: An organizer can receive a topic, consider its relevance and explain whether it shaped the plan. Adoption is not the only evidence of consideration, but a polite acknowledgment alone does not establish what was examined. The later account should make the actual response understandable rather than claim all input changed the outcome.

items.title: Examine participation rather than infer it
items.body: A known partner and an available meeting do not supply every affected voice. Ask what perspectives and supports are actually relevant and available. This keeps inclusion connected to practical opportunity without demanding private cultural disclosure or treating a quiet person as disengaged.

tabs.label: Attendance equals influence
tabs.body: Count a person’s attendance as proof their views shaped the work. This skips the actual contribution and decision response. Attendance can be one observation, but a meaningful account of influence needs to identify what changed or how input was considered.

tabs.label: Partnership equals delegated decision
tabs.body: Call the proposal collaborative and assume Edda may approve a service policy for everyone. That invents both agency delegation and universal representation. Clarify her particular contribution and the actual decision responsibility rather than treating a positive label as authority.

tabs.label: Explain purpose and response
tabs.body: Tell people what the contribution is for, what influence is actually available and how consideration will be explained. This supports a more honest invitation without promising adoption of every suggestion. Practical supports, information handling and missing perspectives still need examination.

Treat attendance as proof of every person’s influence.
check.feedbackCorrect: The invitation names a particular contribution and its proposed consideration without creating a service decision power or guarantee.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Every suggestion cannot be promised as policy from this case. Edda’s role does not establish agency delegation. Attendance alone does not show what input was given, considered or changed.

image.caption: Two people review a printed document together; one points to a line on the page.

intro.heading: Respond to concerns through the appropriate responsibilities
intro.body:
Tobin and Edda’s disagreement concerns how a proposed discussion begins. The example does not make it a protected-class allegation, a misconduct finding or an actual service complaint. Understanding its cultural meanings helps reconsider the response. It does not authorize a staff member to dismiss a different concern as merely cultural or to assume every disagreement follows the same formal route.

Consider a separate practice case. Vale is a supervisor who receives an allegation that an employee was mocked because of national origin. The employee also hopes for a respectful working relationship. MMB Policy 1436 requires managers and supervisors immediately to report all allegations or incidents of protected-class harassment or discrimination to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. Vale does not wait for a partner dialogue, a cultural explanation, the consultant’s agreement or proof of a violation.

Vale follows the agency’s actual complaint and investigation procedures. The report is an allegation, not a finding. Authorized assigned investigation responsibilities remain; a learning conversation neither supplies new authority nor bans an actual assigned role. Nonretaliation applies, including conduct meant to stop a person from reporting or participating in an investigation. Calling the concern a misunderstanding does not resolve those responsibilities.

In the engagement work, Edda can offer a perspective and the consultant can offer leadership, guidance, knowledge and feedback. Staff remain responsible for carrying out their work through actual roles and processes. Seeking help can build capability without requiring every analysis or contribution to pass a consultant approval gate. Relevant DHS equity requirements likewise retain their actual scope; an optional classroom exchange does not replace formal analysis or agency responsibility.

Privately separate the two practice situations and their responses. You do not need to submit a real conflict or allegation to complete the lesson. If applying it at work, identify the actual concern and relevant role rather than deciding the route from a person’s identity or a general cultural label. A respectful relationship and a proper formal response can both matter without one being conditioned on the other.

lessons.keyStatement: Continue respectful inquiry while carrying out the responsibility the actual situation requires.

items.title: Keep the concerns distinct
items.body: Tobin and Edda need clarification of a proposed participation method. Vale has a specific national-origin allegation in a supervisor role. Treating both as ordinary style differences would erase the second case’s duty; treating every method disagreement as a proven violation would invent a finding the first case does not supply.

items.title: Follow the immediate route without a finding
items.body: Vale reports the allegation immediately to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follows actual procedures. She can accurately distinguish what was reported from what an authorized process later finds. A desired apology or repaired relationship is not a prerequisite to the report.

items.title: Use support to develop capability
items.body: A consultant’s feedback or partner perspective can help staff examine work more carefully. It does not make the supporter the owner of every task or a permission gate for actual reporting. Staff should clarify their own responsibility and use relevant support without outsourcing the substantive work.

tabs.label: Call every concern a cultural misunderstanding
tabs.body: Use the course’s meaning inquiry to dismiss Vale’s national-origin allegation. That confuses a useful learning lens with a decision about a formal concern. Her specific manager or supervisor duty remains even when understanding, intent or the final finding is not settled.

tabs.label: Wait for relationship repair
tabs.body: Delay Vale’s report until the employee and colleague agree to continue together. This makes a relationship outcome a condition of required action. The immediate reporting duty and nonretaliation protections retain their actual basis; agreement is not a substitute.

tabs.label: Identify the concern and actual role
tabs.body: Clarify the engagement disagreement in its own terms and respond to Vale’s separate allegation through the specified route. This preserves meaningful cultural inquiry without overgeneralizing it. Partner and consultant support can help staff while actual duties, decisions and procedures stay clear.

check.question: What distinguishes the two cases?
check.correct: The method disagreement needs inquiry; Vale’s supervisor receipt of a national-origin allegation triggers the specified immediate reporting duty.
wrong: Both can be resolved only by waiting for cultural agreement.
Every proposed method disagreement proves harassment.
Consultant approval is required before Vale reports.
check.feedbackCorrect: The distinction connects the response to the supplied concern and actual role without inventing a finding or support gate.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Cultural agreement cannot replace Vale’s immediate duty. A method disagreement does not prove harassment; the supplied concern and role determine the response. The reporting route does not depend on a consultant’s permission.

Examine how the proposed input will be considered.

intro.heading: Return an honest account and keep learning
intro.body:
In the example, Tobin and Edda try a revised explanation of the proposed discussion with three adult readers. Reader A says the distinction between a general opening question and follow-up questions is now clear. Reader B asks who will decide which suggested topics are used. Reader C asks what participation supports would be available. No final event, complete community response or actual service decision is supplied.

These responses show different things. A gives a particular interpretation of the sequence. B identifies an unresolved decision-role question. C identifies a practical participation question whose answer remains open. None of these people is established as representing all affected contributors. Their notes are useful to the proposal without proving universal clarity, access, agreement or delivered engagement.

A fitting account back could explain the changed opening sequence, the available topic contribution and the decision responsibility actually confirmed. It should also retain the open support question and describe the next appropriate inquiry rather than invent availability. MMB’s practical engagement guidance encourages a feedback loop. That means making the consideration understandable; it does not require publication of private names or guarantee every suggestion is adopted.

If a later event occurs or a proposal shapes work, those results need their own evidence. Receiving a topic, considering it, adopting it and delivering a change are distinct. A suggestion not adopted may still have been considered if the reason is honestly explained. Missing feedback stays unknown rather than proving no concerns. A partnership can remain worthwhile while some practical disagreement continues.

Privately identify one supported improvement and one remaining question. You can also reflect on how your own sense of recognition or authorship widened through the full example, without recording a biography or a work result. If you choose an actual application, use proportionate information and real responsibilities. The job aid helps retain these distinctions rather than turn community partnership into a personal cultural score.

How should the review close?
lessons.keyStatement: Close the exchange with an account that is as specific and limited as the evidence.

items.title: Read each account for what it says
items.body: A describes clearer question timing, B asks who chooses topics and C asks about supports. Keep those different accounts distinct. Calling all three satisfied would erase two open questions; calling the revised sequence useless would erase A’s specific useful feedback.

items.title: Explain consideration and remaining responsibility
items.body: A follow-through account can show what input was heard, how it affected the proposal and what still needs examination. If a topic was not adopted, explain the relevant reason rather than claim that listening guarantees adoption. Use the actual decision responsibility and information practices, not an invented representative role.

items.title: Keep learning wider than a final event
items.body: A changed interpretation and clearer invitation can be meaningful even before a discussion is held. Private self-understanding is also valid. These are different from delivered engagement or service outcomes, so describe them as learning and proposal changes rather than using them as proof of a complete result.

tabs.label: Three notes equal community agreement
tabs.body: Describe the readers as the community and claim everyone accepts the plan. This inflates both representation and result. A particular reader’s clarity does not answer the other role and support questions or supply views from people whose feedback is missing.

tabs.label: Open questions erase all progress
tabs.body: Because B and C still have questions, report that the exchange produced no useful change. This discards A’s specific sequence feedback and the widened partner interpretations. Keep the useful progress and unresolved matters together rather than making the account wholly positive or wholly negative.

tabs.label: Return a specific and limited account
tabs.body: Describe the clearer sequence, role question and support question separately, then explain consideration and the appropriate next inquiry. This makes follow-through understandable without inventing a final event or consensus. Private insight can be retained without disclosing personal meanings publicly.

check.question: Which closing account fits the three responses?
check.correct: A reports clearer sequence; B’s decision-role question and C’s support question remain open, with no complete community result supplied.
wrong: All affected people approve because three readers responded.
No progress occurred because two questions remain.
The revised explanation proves the event was delivered accessibly.
check.feedbackCorrect: The account preserves each particular response and its limit without inflating representation or erasing supported progress.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Three readers are not every affected person. Open questions do not erase A’s feedback or learning. A revised explanation does not establish a delivered event or complete access result.

B asks who selects the suggested topics.

The available participation supports need clarification.

A final event has been delivered.

sections.heading: Hear the disagreement
items: Name the proposed methods and separate them from initial judgments about intent.
Receive a person’s chosen account without demanding a biography or assigning a cultural type.
Show what the offered meaning changes in the interpretation and actual invitation.

sections.heading: Clarify participation
items: Explain the actual purpose, available influence and decision responsibility before requesting input.
Distinguish received input, considered input, adopted proposals and delivered changes.
Examine whose perspectives, language and access needs remain missing without inferring them from identity or silence.

sections.heading: Carry out actual responsibilities
items: Identify the relevant concern and real role; a method disagreement is not a proven violation or a universal formal route.

Managers and supervisors immediately report all protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow actual assigned procedures.
Staff own their work; partner contributions and consultant leadership, guidance and feedback support capability without replacing duties or creating a mandatory approval gate.

sections.heading: Follow through and learn
items: Return an understandable account of what was heard, considered, changed and left open within appropriate information responsibilities.
Do not make three responses a community mandate, missing feedback reassurance or a proposal proof of delivery.
Use a private reflection, the complete practice path or an appropriate work application.
